overview.summary: You are curating levels for a node-puzzle game. Levels are produced by level_generator/generate.py, a CLI that uses level_generator/level_verifier/ (a separate, frozen solver/verifier) as a correctness oracle. You do not write puzzle logic by hand: you invoke the generator to produce candidate level JSON files, inspect their metadata (and, when needed, their actual solutions via the verifier CLI), and decide which candidates are worth keeping in the shipped level pool.
overview.working_directory: All commands below assume your shell's cwd is level_generator/, located at the absolute path: C:\Users\prote\Applications\godot\projects\gamedev-jam-2026\tools\level_generator (that directory contains generate.py, test_generate.py, README.md, LEVEL_CURATOR_AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.xml (this file), a levels/ output directory, and the level_verifier/ subdirectory). generate.py locates level_verifier/ relative to its own file path, so cwd doesn't strictly matter for generate.py itself, but level_verifier/verify.py (used below for manual review) DOES require being invoked from inside level_verifier/, since it is a flat, non-package module set with bare-name imports.
overview.environment: Tested against Python 3.10.12; nothing in generate.py or level_verifier/ uses syntax newer than that (f-strings, dataclasses, type hints -- all 3.7+-safe), so any reasonably current Python 3 should work. No pip install is required anywhere in this project: generate.py's imports are argparse, itertools, json, os, random, signal, sys, collections, and typing -- all standard library. level_verifier/'s own modules (model.py, solver.py, reach.py, notation.py, minimality.py, signature.py, api.py) are likewise standard-library-only (mainly dataclasses/typing/json). signal.SIGALRM (used internally by generate.py's timeout wrapper) is POSIX-only -- this project is not expected to run on native Windows Python, only inside a Unix-like shell (WSL, a Linux/macOS sandbox, etc.).

two_tools_you_have.tool: Produces candidate levels. This is your primary interface.

The underlying oracle's own CLI. generate.py already calls this library's functions internally to filter/score/emit candidates, so you do NOT need verify.py to determine solvability or minimality -- that is already decided before a file is ever written. You DO need verify.py to actually SEE a solution (generate.py's output JSON never contains rendered solution steps, by design, so that curating a level doesn't force you to look at its answer) and as an independent second opinion if you want one.

pipeline.name: deletion
pipeline.description: Delta-debugging shrink. Produces exactly ONE level per invocation: starts from a randomly over-provisioned pool of inputs/operations against a FIXED set of output targets you specify, then greedily deletes nodes that don't break solvability. Minimal by construction. To get multiple candidates toward the same output targets, invoke it repeatedly with different --seed values -- each seed yields a different minimal level from the same starting shape.

flags.flag: Comma-separated output target values, e.g. "1,17,19". Determines the number of outputs (1-4) and their exact values. This is the one thing Pipeline A does NOT search over -- you choose it.
Size of the starting input pool before shrinking (final level will have <= this many inputs, usually fewer).
Size of the starting operation pool before shrinking (final level will have <= this many ops).

Comma-separated list restricting which op types are eligible to be sampled into the starting pool. Use this to bias what mechanic a level teaches -- e.g. "subtract,store" to exclude add/sum entirely, forcing a subtract-and-latch level.
Controls both the random starting pool AND the deletion order. Different seeds against the same --outputs/--pool-* produce different minimal levels.
"lo,hi". Range the randomly-sampled starting input pool is drawn from. Purely a display/design-constraint range -- unrelated to --bound (see the dedicated ranges section below).

"lo,hi". EVERY value in --outputs is validated against this range up front, before any generation is attempted -- an out-of-range --outputs value now fails fast with a clear message and exit code 1, rather than silently running a full generation attempt that comes back "unsolvable" for reasons that have nothing to do with solvability. See "Range validation" below.
"lo,hi". Range randomly-sampled 'add' op values are drawn from when --op-types includes add.

Value bound "lo,hi" passed to the verifier's solve(). Deliberately tighter than the verifier's own internal default (-200,200) -- see "Performance characteristics" below before widening this. This is the SOLVER's intermediate-value search space, NOT a value- acceptance range -- it is independent of --input-range/ --output-range/--add-value-range and does not need to match them. Widen --bound freely for solver headroom without it affecting what values get sampled, accepted, or emitted.
Max store-latch events the solver will search through.
Soft target for how many distinct solution families the post-hoc family-count search aims for (affects search budget, not a hard cap -- actual counts can exceed this).
Wall-clock seconds the generator will wait on any single verifier call before giving up and treating it as inconclusive. Set to 0 to disable (not recommended -- see performance notes).
Flips the sign of the family-count term in the difficulty score. Off (default): more solution families make a level score EASIER (more forgiving). On: more families score HARDER (richer).
Base filename (and in-file "name" field) for the emitted level.
Directory the JSON file is written into (created if missing). Point this at your curated pool directory, or a scratch directory for review-before-promotion -- your choice.

pipeline.caveat: Pipeline A does NOT discard or resample a level whose output equals one of its own input values (a "trivial" one-wire solution) -- it only prints a warning to stderr and still writes the file. Check the emitted level's own "inputs"/"outputs" JSON fields for overlap yourself before accepting a Pipeline-A level; don't rely on stderr output, which you may not see if you're invoking this programmatically.

pipeline.name: enumerate
pipeline.description: Forward enumeration with derived targets. Fixes an EXACT operation set (you specify types and count) and an input set, computes what output values are actually reachable (accounting for store ratcheting across multiple latches), and searches candidate output tuples drawn from that reachable set -- never guessing blind. Can emit MANY levels in a single invocation (all sharing the same input/op shape, differing only in output targets), ranked and numbered by difficulty score.

flags.flag: Number of inputs (1-4).

Comma-separated explicit input values, count must match --inputs. Omit to let the generator pick random distinct values from --input-range. If given explicitly, EVERY value is now validated against --input-range and rejected outright (clear message, exit 1) if any value falls outside it -- see "Range validation" below.

Comma-separated op types IN ID-ASSIGNMENT ORDER, e.g. "sum,subtract,store,store" -> produces P1(sum), M1(subtract), S1(store), S2(store). For "add" ops, append a fixed value with a colon: "add:5,store" -> A1 with value 5. Unlike Pipeline A, there is NO automatic cap on how many combinational (add/sum/subtract) ops you request here -- see performance caveat below. An explicit "add:N" value IS now validated against --add-value-range -- an out-of-range N raises ValueError (uncaught -- traceback, exit 1; see the exit-codes section), same failure style as an unknown op type already had.

Max output tuple SIZE to try; the search sweeps sizes 1..this. If you want ONLY N-output levels, you must post-filter the emitted files yourself for len(outputs)==N -- there is no "exact size" flag, and with a low --max-emit the smaller sizes can crowd out larger ones before the sweep even reaches them (see below).

Skips two things at once: (1) the spec's node-forcing "covering" pre-filter, which otherwise discards the ENTIRE (inputs, ops) pairing outright if even one node can never be forced into any solution within the design value range -- this is common and can silently produce zero survivors in default mode even for reasonable-looking op sets; (2) the fast-path assumption that covering implies minimality. With --exhaustive, every candidate output tuple gets a real leave-one-out minimality check instead.
If a plain `enumerate` call reports "No levels survived... some node could never be forced," retry the same command with --exhaustive before concluding the (inputs, ops) shape doesn't work -- this is the single most common gotcha with Pipeline B.

Only affects --input-values selection when you don't supply your own, and the add-value fallback when an "add:N" isn't given a value. Does NOT reorder the enumeration search itself (that's deterministic over the reachable value range).
Same meaning as Pipeline A -- also the range --input-values entries are validated against.

"lo,hi". THIS IS THE TARGET-ENUMERATION RANGE for Pipeline B -- what output values get considered as candidates at all (previously a hardcoded, unconfigurable -20..20 literal). Independent of --bound: you can widen --bound for solver headroom on intermediates while keeping --output-range narrow for display-safe targets, or vice versa. There is no separate validation step here the way Pipeline A has one for --outputs, because Pipeline B never accepts a raw output value from you in the first place -- it only ever proposes values already drawn from --output-range.
Same meaning as Pipeline A -- also the range explicit "add:N" values in --ops are validated against.
Same meaning as Pipeline A -- the solver's search space, independent of the three ranges above.
Same meaning as Pipeline A.
Same meaning as Pipeline A.
Same meaning as Pipeline A, but applied per-probe during the reachability setup too (see performance notes) -- a LOT of small solve() calls happen before any level is even considered.

Stops the search after this many surviving levels. This is a SAFETY VALVE on a search space that can reach ~100k candidate tuples (per the design spec's own sizing estimate) -- raise it if you want a bigger batch to choose from, but expect proportionally longer runtime.
Same meaning as Pipeline A.
Base name; ranked survivors are automatically suffixed "_1", "_2", ... in ascending difficulty-score order (rank 1 = easiest).
Same meaning as Pipeline A.

pipeline.behavior_note: Unlike Pipeline A, Pipeline B silently discards (does not emit, does not warn) any candidate whose output value equals an input value -- you never need to check for that case with Pipeline B output.

value_ranges.description: Three independently configurable ranges replace what used to be a single, unconfigurable -20..20 "design range" -- added specifically so this tool can be retuned for a game's actual display constraints (node values that are too wide overflow the UI) without a source edit.
value_ranges.range: Where randomly-sampled starting inputs are drawn from (both pipelines); Pipeline B's --input-values entries are validated against it when supplied explicitly.
Pipeline A: --outputs values outside it are rejected outright, before any generation is attempted. Pipeline B: the TARGET-ENUMERATION range -- what output values get proposed as candidates at all.
Where randomly-sampled 'add' op values come from; explicit "add:N" values in Pipeline B's --ops are validated against it too.
value_ranges.decoupled_from_bound: --bound is the SOLVER's intermediate-value search space (how wide a value solve() will consider mid-network while proving solvability) -- a performance/completeness knob, structurally unrelated to what values are acceptable as inputs/outputs/add-values in the emitted level. Widening --bound gives the solver more room to find a solution; it does NOT widen what gets sampled, validated, or accepted. You can freely combine a wide --bound with narrow --input-range/--output-range/ --add-value-range (generous solver headroom, display-safe output), or any other combination. Do not assume these move together just because they defaulted to the same numbers in an earlier version of this tool.
value_ranges.negative_lower_bound_gotcha: All four "lo,hi" flags (--bound included) need --flag=lo,hi (WITH the '=') whenever lo is negative. `--output-range -9,20` (space-separated) is misparsed by argparse as an attempt to pass an unrecognized new flag, because argparse's heuristic for "is this a value or another flag?" only recognizes bare negative INTEGERS (matching `-9`) as values, not "-9,20" (the comma breaks that pattern) -- you'll see "error: argument --output-range: expected one argument". This was already true of --bound before this change; it's just far more likely to bite now, since three more flags default to a negative lower bound that you may routinely want to override. Always use the '=' form for these four flags when lo is negative: `--output-range=-9,20`, not `--output-range -9,20`.

output_format.description: Every emitted file is a verifier-loadable level JSON (openable directly via level_verifier/verify.py or level_from_dict()) with one extra top-level key, "generator", holding curation-relevant metadata. Field meanings:
output_format.field: Level's display/file-base name.
{id: value} -- compare against "outputs" yourself for trivial-output overlap on Pipeline-A files (see caveat above).
{id: {type[, value for add]}}.
{id: value} -- the fixed goal state.
"deletion" or "enumerate".
Seed used (or a custom string if you hand-curated/re-emitted a level -- see "manual re-emission" below).

The EXACT search budget every solvability/minimality claim in this file rests on. Treat these as load-bearing: if you re-verify this level with verify.py, pass matching --bound/--max-latches, or you may get a different (and differently-costly) answer. See performance notes.

[lo, hi] lists recording the three value-acceptance ranges in force when this level was generated (see the dedicated ranges section below). Independent of generator.bound -- a level can perfectly well have a wide bound and narrow ranges, or vice versa. These are what you check to confirm a level's node values are actually safe for your current display constraints; generator.bound tells you nothing about that.

true / false / null. NULL specifically means the final minimality sanity-check itself timed out during generation -- the level's own generation process still believes it's minimal, but that belief is UNCONFIRMED. Treat null the same as "needs manual re-check" before shipping, not as a pass.

Whether every leave-one-out check behind the minimality claim actually proved its result within bound/max_latches (true), or merely ran out of search budget without finding a counterexample (false) -- still directionally trustworthy for "this node is required," but not a completeness proof. null if minimal_within_bound is also null.
Rendered step-notation line count of the simplest known solution family. Rough proxy for how long a playthrough takes.
Store-latch events in the simplest known solution. Rough proxy for how much of the "ratcheting" mechanic a level exercises.
Distinct solution families found (destination-based, symmetry-aware -- see level_verifier/notation.py). null means this specific search timed out; see generator.solver_timeout_hit.
Whether the family-count search proved it found ALL families within budget, or just stopped early.

Integer 1-5 (never 6 or higher -- see below), computed from the SAME three raw fields already in this JSON (solution_length, latch_count, solution_family_count). The exact formula, verified directly against generate.py:
fam_term = -(solution_family_count - 1) # negated by default; # positive if the level # was generated with # --richer-families-are-harder score = solution_length + 2*latch_count + fam_term tier = 1 if score <= 4 = 2 if score <= 8 = 3 if score <= 12 = 4 if score <= 17 = 5 otherwise # score > 17; there is no tier 6
generator.tier is ALREADY a function of solution_length + latch_count + family_count. If your own tiering logic also derives a tier from those same three fields, you are recomputing the same signal twice under two names. Pick one: either (a) trust generator.tier as-is and treat it as the level's tier, or (b) ignore generator.tier entirely and compute your own tier from the three raw fields using your own formula/thresholds -- do not feed generator.tier as a FOURTH input into a formula that already consumes the three fields it was built from, and do not treat agreement between the two as independent confirmation of anything; they are mathematically coupled, not two opinions.
If your design calls for six tiers, generator.tier's heuristic as shipped can only ever emit 1-5 -- tier 6 is structurally unreachable under the current TIER_THRESHOLDS = [4, 8, 12, 17] in generate.py (four thresholds partition the score line into five buckets, by construction). There is no hidden tier-6 case being suppressed elsewhere. To get a sixth tier you would need to either: split one of the existing five buckets by adding a threshold (e.g. inside generate.py's TIER_THRESHOLDS list, which is explicitly documented in README.md as "an arbitrary, documented default; tune to taste"), or define your six-tier mapping independently from the three raw fields rather than from generator.tier. Decide which before writing curator instructions that assume six tiers exist in the data today -- they don't.

true if ANY verifier call anywhere during this level's generation hit the wall-clock --solve-timeout. A distinct, generator-owned incompleteness layer on top of bound/max_latches -- true here is a signal to double-check this specific level manually before trusting its other metadata fields at face value.
(deletion only) How many random starting pools were tried before one was solvable.
(deletion only) Whether every deletion-loop solvability check during shrinking proved its result within budget.
(enumerate only) Whether --exhaustive was used for this candidate.
(enumerate only) Whether the reachability computation behind this level's candidacy proved its result within budget.

generator_exit_codes_and_failure_behavio.description: generate.py's exit-code contract is thinner than verify.py's, and one case in particular is easy to misread. Verified directly by running each scenario below and inspecting the actual exit code, stdout, stderr, and whether --out-dir was created.

case.name: success (Pipeline A wrote a level, or Pipeline B wrote 1+ levels)
case.behavior: Normal "Wrote <path> ..." line(s) on stdout, one or more JSON files exist under --out-dir.

case.name: Pipeline A: resample attempts exhausted (no solvable starting pool found within max_resamples=200)
case.behavior: stderr: "Failed to find a solvable starting pool after max resamples; try a different --seed or larger --pool-inputs/--pool-ops." Nothing is written; --out-dir is not even created if it didn't already exist. This is an explicit, intentional sys.exit(1) -- not a crash.

case.name: Pipeline B: zero survivors
case.behavior: THIS IS THE CASE YOUR §10 NEEDS TO KNOW ABOUT. "Zero survivors" is NOT an error from generate.py's point of view -- it exits 0, exactly like success. stderr gets a message: "No levels survived enumeration for this (inputs, ops) pairing -- either nothing was solvable, or (in fast-path mode) some node could never be forced within the design range." --out-dir is never created (no makedirs call happens on this path) and stdout is empty. You CANNOT distinguish "ran successfully, found nothing" from "ran successfully, found something" by exit code alone for Pipeline B -- you must check whether --out-dir exists / contains new files, or match stderr for that literal string. (Retrying with --exhaustive is the standard next step here, per the interface doc's Pipeline B recommendation.)

case.name: malformed CLI input the parser doesn't specifically validate (e.g. non-integer in --outputs, unknown op type in --ops, --pool-inputs larger than the available distinct-value range)
case.behavior: An UNCAUGHT Python exception (ValueError, typically) propagates out of main() with a full traceback printed to stderr -- there is no top-level try/except in generate.py. This is functionally a crash, distinguishable from the two intentional exit(1) cases above by stderr containing a Python traceback (the words "Traceback (most recent call last)") rather than one of the two friendly one-line messages quoted above.

case.name: --input-values count doesn't match --inputs (enumerate only)
case.behavior: stderr: "--input-values count must match --inputs" (via an explicit `raise SystemExit(...)`, not a traceback).

case.name: --outputs (deletion) or --input-values (enumerate) contains a value outside the configured range
case.behavior: A clean, single-line stderr message via `raise SystemExit(...)`, NOT a traceback -- e.g. "--outputs contains values outside the configured output range [-9,20] (--output-range): [50]". No files written, --out-dir not created. This is the new validation added for the display-range work: previously an out-of-range --outputs value would run a full generation attempt and come back "unsolvable," which read as ordinary failure rather than the input error it was -- that's fixed; check for this message pattern to distinguish "you gave a value outside the allowed range" from a genuine solvability failure.

case.name: explicit add:N value in --ops (enumerate) is outside --add-value-range
case.behavior: Unlike the two cases above, this one IS a traceback (uncaught ValueError raised from build_fixed_ops -- matches the existing "unknown op type" failure style, not the clean-message style used for --outputs/--input-values). Message: "add value N for '<id>' is outside the configured add-value range [lo,hi] (--add-value-range)". Distinguish from a genuinely malformed --ops string by this specific wording appearing in the traceback's final line.

generator_exit_codes_and_failure_behavio.summary_rule: To reliably classify a generate.py run: (1) check exit code -- 0 means either real success OR Pipeline-B zero-survivors, both need the output-directory check to disambiguate; nonzero always means something went wrong. (2) On nonzero, check stderr for one of the two known friendly messages above (intentional, actionable failures) versus a Python traceback (malformed input -- fix the command, don't retry as-is). (3) On zero, check whether --out-dir gained the file(s) you expected; if not, it was Pipeline B's zero-survivors case, not a crash.

corpus_calibration.description: Confirmed directly: level_verifier/tests_corpus.py's CASES list IS the designer's five-case regression corpus from spec section 8 -- run via `python3 verify.py --test` from inside level_verifier/. It embeds all five cases as Python dicts (name, inputs, operations, outputs, plus expect_solvable/expect_minimal), so `--test` is fully self-contained and requires no external files to run.
corpus_calibration.standalone_files_available: If your calibration step wants standalone level JSON files (e.g. to feed through generate.py's own tooling, or to diff against, rather than just running --test and reading pass/fail) -- you do NOT need to build these by hand. They already exist at level_verifier/test_cases/case1.json through case5.json, and are byte-for-byte the same level data embedded in tests_corpus.py (verified by direct comparison). Use these as your calibration fixtures directly.
corpus_calibration.stale_reference_warning: level_verifier/README.md itself refers to a "levels/" directory as holding "the regression corpus as standalone level JSON files" -- that directory does not exist in this checkout. The real location is test_cases/, confirmed above. Don't let an agent go looking for level_verifier/levels/; it isn't there.
corpus_calibration.expected_output: `python3 verify.py --test` (run from inside level_verifier/) prints a per-case trace ending in the literal line "ALL TESTS PASSED" on success, exit code 0. On any failure it reports which case(s) failed and exits nonzero -- treat that as the "generated content is untrusted this session" gate your §4 already specifies.

pipeline_a_sampling_behavior.description: Verified directly against generate.py's actual sampling code and by running edge-case commands, since Pipeline B documents its distinctness behavior in the interface doc but Pipeline A's was previously left implicit. Updated for the value-ranges change -- range is now enforced where it previously wasn't; distinctness still isn't.
pipeline_a_sampling_behavior.fact: Drawn from --add-value-range (default -9..9; random_op_pool's add_value_range parameter defaults to DEFAULT_ADD_VALUE_RANGE, and both CLI subcommands now expose --add-value-range to override it).

Guaranteed distinct by construction: random_distinct_values() samples without replacement from --input-range (shuffle-then-take-n), so it is structurally impossible for Pipeline A's randomly-sampled starting inputs to collide.

NOW VALIDATED (this was previously the biggest gap in this section, and is exactly what the value-ranges change fixed). Every value in --outputs is checked against --output-range up front, in cmd_deletion, before any generation is attempted; any value outside it produces a clean `raise SystemExit(...)` message and exit code 1, with nothing written -- see the exit-codes section's dedicated case for this. The same applies to Pipeline B's --input-values against --input-range, and to explicit "add:N" values in Pipeline B's --ops against --add-value-range (that last one raises ValueError/traceback rather than a clean SystemExit -- see exit-codes section).

STILL NOT validated -- this part of the original gap remains. parse_int_list() does a bare int() conversion with no dedup check, and the Level object Pipeline A builds is constructed directly (not via level_from_dict()), which means the verifier's own distinctness warning-check (validate(), which only ever WARNS even when it does run) is never invoked on generator output at all. Confirmed by direct test: `--outputs 5,5` (with values inside --output-range) still exits 0 and happily writes a level with O1=5, O2=5. In practice this is nearly always self-defeating rather than dangerous: a duplicate output value means any single value that satisfies one target automatically satisfies the other, so Pipeline A's own delta-debugging shrink will typically collapse straight down to a trivial one-input, zero-op level (which DOES still trigger the existing trivial-output stderr warning, since that input value now also equals an output value) -- but nothing currently stops --outputs "3,3" from being accepted and emitted if you don't check for it yourself. If your curation pipeline wants a hard guarantee here, check --outputs for duplicates yourself before invoking generate.py, or re-run level_from_dict() on the emitted JSON afterward and check .warnings == [] the way test_generate.py's own regression suite does.

verifier_interactions.description: Use level_verifier/verify.py directly when you need to actually SEE a solution (to judge whether it's interesting/fun, not just "valid"), or want an independent second opinion outside the generator's own pipeline. All commands below assume `cd level_verifier` first.

command.purpose: full human-readable report (solvability + a solution + minimality table)
just the first/simplest solution, rendered as step notation
every distinct solution family (use to judge how 'open' vs 'directed' a level feels)
leave-one-out minimality table only, no solution shown
run the verifier's OWN regression suite (only needed if you suspect level_verifier/ itself is broken -- you should never need to touch its code)

verifier_interactions.exit_codes: 0 = solvable and minimal. 1 = unsolvable within the given bound. 2 = solvable but not minimal. Useful for scripting a quick pass/fail triage across many candidate files without parsing text output.
verifier_interactions.critical_caveat: ALWAYS pass --bound and --max-latches matching the values recorded in the level's own generator.bound / generator.max_latches fields (verify.py's --bound takes a single N for [-N,N], or "lo,hi" -- e.g. bound [-20,20] in the JSON becomes --bound -20,20 on the command line). verify.py's OWN default bound is (-200,200), much wider than the generator's default (-20,20), and unlike generate.py, verify.py has NO wall-clock timeout protection. Running it at a wider bound than the level was generated under risks reproducing the same reach_values() combinatorial blowup documented in README.md's "performance characteristics" section -- observed taking 20+ seconds, in the worst case effectively hanging, on nothing more exotic than a handful of subtract/sum ops. Matching the recorded bound avoids this entirely and is also the only way to get an answer consistent with what the generator itself claimed.

performance_characteristics.note: This section is operational, not optional reading -- both pipelines can appear to "hang" if you push past these limits, and that is a known, documented characteristic of the underlying (frozen) verifier, not a bug to work around by killing and retrying blindly.
performance_characteristics.fact: The verifier's solve() gets combinatorially slower as combinational (add/sum/subtract) op COUNT increases in a single level -- NOT just as bound widens. Measured: 3 combinational ops stayed under ~2s per call; going to 4 pushed a single call from ~2s to ~20s with barely any change in states explored. Pipeline A enforces a cap of 3 combinational ops per randomly-sampled pool automatically. Pipeline B's --ops has NO such cap, because you're choosing the exact op set deliberately -- if you ask for 4+ combinational ops, expect each solve() call to be significantly slower, and raise --solve-timeout accordingly rather than assuming something is broken.

Pipeline B's `enumerate` setup phase (computing what's reachable, and what requires each individual node) issues on the order of (node_count + 1) x 41 individual solve() probes BEFORE any candidate output tuple is even considered. For a 6-node shape this took ~2-5s in testing; it scales with node count and with --solve-timeout (a probe that times out still costs the full timeout).

A timeout is a THIRD outcome, never treated as a proof of solvability or unsolvability by the generator -- but it IS treated conservatively (as "not solvable" / "node not required") in the moment, which can cause the generator to keep a node it didn't strictly need to, or skip a candidate that might actually have worked. generator.solver_timeout_hit is your signal to re-check such a level manually (with a higher --solve-timeout, or via verify.py at the SAME bound/max_latches) before fully trusting its metadata.

curator_responsibilities_not_handled_by_.item:
The generator's isomorphism filter (canonical_signature / IsomorphismFilter in generate.py) only dedupes WITHIN a single `enumerate` invocation's survivor list. It does NOT persist across separate CLI calls, across different --seed values, across Pipeline A runs, or against levels already sitting in your curated pool / --out-dir. If you run the generator multiple times (which you will, routinely), you are responsible for checking new candidates against your existing pool yourself. You can reuse the generator's own logic as a library rather than reimplementing it:
import sys, os, json LEVEL_GENERATOR_DIR = "/absolute/path/to/level_generator" sys.path.insert(0, LEVEL_GENERATOR_DIR) sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(LEVEL_GENERATOR_DIR, "level_verifier")) import generate as g from api import level_from_dict # api.py is level_verifier's own re-export seam
seen = set() for path in existing_pool_paths: level = level_from_dict(json.load(open(path))) seen.add(g.canonical_signature(level))
new_level = level_from_dict(json.load(open(candidate_path))) is_duplicate = g.canonical_signature(new_level) in seen
An earlier version of this snippet added only LEVEL_GENERATOR_DIR to sys.path and imported `from model import level_from_dict` directly. Tested directly: that line does NOT raise ImportError, but only by accident -- `import generate as g` has a side effect of adding level_verifier/ to sys.path itself (generate.py's own top-level code does this unconditionally, so it can import its own dependencies), and `from model import level_from_dict` was silently riding on that side effect rather than being correct on its own terms. Two fixes applied above: (1) add level_verifier/ to sys.path explicitly rather than relying on an import order you'd have to remember, and (2) import level_from_dict from api (level_verifier's own re-export module, purpose-built as the stable seam for exactly this kind of external use) rather than reaching into model.py directly -- api.py re-exports level_from_dict unchanged, so this is a drop-in swap, not a behavior change.

curator_responsibilities_not_handled_by_.item: See the caveat under the deletion pipeline above -- Pipeline A does not self-filter this; Pipeline B does.

The generator's tier/score is a heuristic over (solution_length, latch_count, family_count). It has no notion of whether a level is fun, whether its solution path is intuitive vs. fiddly, or whether a "minimal" level is minimal in a way that feels satisfying vs. just technically irreducible. Use verify.py --all on promising candidates to actually inspect the solution family(ies) before committing a level to the shipped pool.

If you hand-pick and re-save a level (e.g., copying a candidate into your curated pool with a new name, or after manually re-verifying it), you can reuse generate.py's own emit_level() function to keep the generator.* metadata block consistently formatted -- see level_generator/generate.py's emit_level() signature, or just hand-edit the JSON's "generator" block directly; level_from_dict() ignores unrecognized top-level/nested keys, so the file stays verifier-loadable either way.

quick_reference_workflow.step: Decide the mechanic/shape you want (op types, input/output counts) based on the tier/mechanic you're targeting.

For a single hand-tuned level with fixed output targets: use `deletion` with a few different --seed values, keep the one you like best. For a batch exploring one fixed mechanic across many possible targets: use `enumerate` (with --exhaustive if the plain covering pass reports zero survivors), raising --max-emit if you want more candidates.

Filter the emitted JSON files: check generator.minimal_within_bound is true (not null), generator.solver_timeout_hit is false (or manually re-check if true), and (for Pipeline A) that inputs/outputs don't overlap.
Deduplicate against your existing pool using canonical_signature (see above) -- the generator will not have done this for you across runs.
For serious candidates, run verify.py --all at the level's own recorded bound/max_latches to actually look at the solution(s) and judge quality/interest.
Promote the survivors into your shipped level pool; discard or re-seed the rest.
